description: We're an Argentine team of developers and data builders turning NASA data into farm decisions. Farmers face erratic climate, scarce water and degraded soil. Ashfield compares 3+ crop rotations, including the current one, explains each and cites its data (POWER soil moisture, GPM rain, MODIS vegetation), and flags uncertainty for a local agronomist to verify. Join a team with a working demo and real validation. We seek an agronomist, remote sensing/statistics and video/design skills.
summary:
Ashfield is a web app that turns NASA Earth data into crop rotation decisions for farmers. The producer outlines a field, splits it into parcels with a crop each, and sets priorities (save water, earn more, avoid stubble burning). Ashfield compares the current rotation with up to three alternatives, and each one explains why it fits, the evidence behind it, expected benefits, information gaps and risks. Every number shows its source, resolution and confidence: NASA POWER (soil moisture, rain, temperature), GPM IMERG (rain), MODIS (vegetation and bare soil), SRTM and GRACE-FO. Each parcel also gets fire, drought, frost and heat indicators, a calendar of vulnerable months and a season-versus-normal timeline.

We validated the satellites against ground data: temperature against 53 weather stations and rain against 25 INTA stations, reporting the real errors. Where data are missing, such as hail, we say so. The tool supports a local agronomist's judgment and never replaces it.

It matters because climate, water scarcity and soil degradation make planting decisions riskier, and NASA data rarely reaches the person standing on the field.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. Ashfield is a decision-support web app for farmers. The producer outlines a field, splits it into parcels with a crop each, and ranks what worries them (drought, frost, heat, El Niño, fire) and what they need (water access, income, soil). Ashfield compares the current crop rotation with up to three alternatives. Each one explains why it fits, the NASA-data evidence behind it, expected benefits, information gaps and risks that a local agronomist must review. Each parcel also gets a calendar of vulnerable and bare-soil months, a season-versus-normal timeline, rain and temperature scenario sliders, and estimated margins from the farmer's own costs.

HOW IT WORKS. A deterministic, explainable engine (20 crops, 12 rotation templates, every datum sourced) filters rotations by frost, water and crop suitability, then ranks them by the farmer's priorities. Evidence comes from NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MODIS, SRTM and GRACE-FO, harmonized on one H3 grid with SoilGrids, Sentinel-2 and INTA data. An LLM only rewrites the engine's numbers in plain language; it never decides.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT. Farmers get NASA data translated to their own field, with fewer stubble burns, less water waste and healthier soil as the goal.

CREATIVITY. Transparency is the design: every number shows source, resolution and confidence, and each diagnosis states how well satellites match ground truth. We validated against 53 weather stations (temperature) and 25 INTA stations (rain), reported the real errors, and dropped SMAP because it failed our quality checks.

FACTORS. Plain language for non-technical users, mobile use, privacy (fields stay in the browser, no accounts, the LLM never sees coordinates), and honest limits. Orin field data were collected before the hackathon; we used only the data.

TOOLS. React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Python, FastAPI, H3, Cloudflare R2, Vercel and the Gemini API. We used AI coding assistants (Claude, Devin) during development.
dataRefs: MODIS MOD13C2 V061 (monthly NDVI, bare-soil days)
NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fires, plot-level fire risk)
projectRefs: Sentinel-2 L2A, ESA Copernicus (via AWS Earth Search): current crop and field moisture zones
SoilGrids, ISRIC (soil texture and organic carbon)
Fields of The World 2025 (field boundaries, CC BY 4.0)
INTA GeoINTA, Mapa Nacional de Cultivos (crop map)
NOAA CPC Oceanic Niño Index (El Niño)
OpenStreetMap (place search, nearby services, base map)
Orin field data: 53 weather stations (collected before the hackathon; data only)
